{{short description|Model of viscous fluid flow between two surfaces moving relative to each other}}

In [[fluid dynamics]], '''Couette flow''' is the flow of a [[viscosity|viscous]] [[fluid]] in the space between two surfaces, one of which is moving [[tangent]]ially relative to the other. The relative motion of the surfaces imposes a [[shear stress]] on the fluid and induces flow. Depending on the definition of the term, there may also be an applied [[pressure gradient]] in the flow direction. 

The Couette configuration models certain practical problems, like the [[Earth's mantle]] and [[Atmosphere of Earth|atmosphere]],<ref>Zhilenko et al. (2018)</ref> and flow in lightly loaded [[Fluid bearing|journal bearings]]. It is also employed in [[Viscometer|viscometry]] and to demonstrate approximations of [[Time reversibility|reversibility]].<ref>Guyon et al. (2001), p. 136</ref><ref>Heller (1960)</ref> 

It is named after [[Maurice Couette]], a Professor of Physics at the French [[University of Angers]] in the late 19th century. [[Isaac Newton]] first defined the problem of Couette flow in Proposition 51 of his ''[[Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica]]'', and expanded upon the ideas in Corollary 2.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Donnelly |first=Russell J. |date=1991-11-01 |title=Taylor-Couette Flow: The Early Days |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article/44/11/32/406407/Taylor-Couette-Flow-The-Early-DaysFluid-caught |journal=Physics Today |language=en |volume=44 |issue=11 |pages=32–39 |bibcode=1991PhT....44k..32D |doi=10.1063/1.881296 |issn=0031-9228|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":16">{{Cite book |last=Rowlands |first=Peter |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=u0NBDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA162 |title=Newton – Innovation And Controversy |publisher=[[World Scientific Publishing]] |year=2017 |isbn=9781786344045 |pages=162}}</ref>

== Planar Couette flow ==

[[File:Laminar shear.svg|thumb|right|300px|Simple Couette configuration using two infinite flat plates.]]
Couette flow is frequently used in undergraduate physics and engineering courses to illustrate [[Shearing (physics)|shear-driven]] fluid motion. A simple configuration corresponds to two infinite, parallel plates separated by a distance <math>h</math>; one plate translates with a constant relative velocity <math>U</math> in its own plane. Neglecting pressure gradients, the [[Navier–Stokes equations]] simplify to

:<math>\frac{d^2 u}{d y^2} = 0,</math>

where <math>y</math> is the spatial coordinate normal to the plates and <math>u(y)</math> is the velocity field. This equation reflects the assumption that the flow is ''unidirectional'' — that is, only one of the three velocity components <math>(u, v, w)</math> is non-trivial. If the lower plate corresponds to <math>y=0</math>, the boundary conditions are <math>u(0)=0</math> and <math>u(h)=U</math>. The exact solution

:<math>u (y) = U\frac{y}{h} </math>

can be found by integrating twice and solving for the constants using the boundary conditions.
A notable aspect of the flow is that [[shear stress]] is constant throughout the domain. In particular, the first derivative of the velocity, <math>U/h</math>, is constant. According to [[Newtonian fluid|Newton's law of viscosity]], the shear stress is the product of this expression and the (constant) fluid [[viscosity]].

===Startup===
[[File:StartupCouette.pdf|thumb|200px|Startup Couette flow]]
In reality, the Couette solution is not reached instantaneously. The "startup problem" describing the approach to steady state is given by

:<math>\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \nu \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2}</math>

subject to the initial condition

:<math>u(y,0)=0, \quad 0<y<h,</math>

and with the same boundary conditions as the steady flow:

:<math>u(0,t)=0, \quad u(h,t)=U, \quad t>0.</math>

The problem can be made [[Homogeneous differential equation|homogeneous]] by subtracting the steady solution. Then, applying [[separation of variables]] leads to the solution:<ref>Pozrikidis (2011), pp. 338–339</ref>

:<math>u(y,t)= U \frac{y}{h} - \frac{2U}{\pi} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n} e^{-n^2 \pi^2 \frac{\nu t}{h^2}} \sin \left[n \pi \left(1-\frac{y}{h}\right)\right]</math>.

The timescale describing relaxation to steady state is <math>t\sim h^2/\nu</math>, as illustrated in the figure. The time required to reach the steady state depends only on the spacing between the plates <math>h</math> and the [[kinematic viscosity]] of the fluid, but not on <math>U</math>.

=== Planar flow with pressure gradient ===
A more general Couette flow includes a constant pressure gradient <math>G=-dp/dx=\mathrm{constant}</math> in a direction parallel to the plates. The Navier–Stokes equations are

:<math>   \frac{d^2 u}{d y^2}  =- \frac{G}{\mu},</math>

where <math>\mu</math> is the [[dynamic viscosity]]. Integrating the above equation twice and applying the boundary conditions (same as in the case of Couette flow without pressure gradient) gives

:<math>u (y) = \frac{G}{2\mu} y \, (h-y) + U \frac{y}{h}.</math>

The pressure gradient can be positive (adverse pressure gradient) or negative (favorable pressure gradient). In the limiting case of stationary plates (<math>U=0</math>), the flow is referred to as [[Hagen–Poiseuille equation#Plane Poiseuille flow|Plane Poiseuille flow]], and has a symmetric (with reference to the horizontal mid-plane) parabolic velocity profile.<ref>Kundu et al. (2016), p. 415</ref>

=== Compressible flow ===
[[File:CompCouette.pdf|thumb|200px|Compressible Couette flow for <math>\mathrm{M}=0</math>]]
[[File:CompCouette2.pdf|thumb|200px|Compressible Couette flow for <math>\mathrm{M}^2\mathrm{Pr}=7.5</math>]]
In [[incompressible flow]], the velocity profile is linear because the fluid temperature is constant. When the upper and lower walls are maintained at different temperatures, the velocity profile is more complicated. However, it has an exact implicit solution as shown by C. R. Illingworth in 1950.<ref>Lagerstrom (1996)</ref>

Consider the plane Couette flow with lower wall at rest and the upper wall in motion with constant velocity <math>U</math>. Denote fluid properties at the lower wall with subscript <math>w</math> and properties at the upper wall with subscript <math>\infty</math>. The properties and the pressure at the upper wall are prescribed and taken as reference quantities. Let <math>l</math> be the distance between the two walls. The boundary conditions are

:<math>u=0, \ v =0, \ h=h_w=c_{pw} T_w \ \text{at} \ y=0,</math>
:<math>u=U, \ v =0, \ h=h_\infty=c_{p\infty} T_\infty, \ p=p_\infty \ \text{at} \ y=l</math>

where <math>h</math> is the [[specific enthalpy]] and <math>c_p</math> is the [[specific heat]]. [[Conservation of mass]] and <math>y</math>-momentum requires <math>v=0, \ p=p_\infty</math> everywhere in the flow domain. [[Conservation of energy]] and <math>x</math>-momentum reduce to

:<math> \frac{d}{dy} \left(\mu \frac{du}{dy}\right) =0, \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d\tau}{dy}=0, \quad \Rightarrow \quad \tau=\tau_w</math>
:<math> \frac{1}{\mathrm{Pr}}\frac{d}{dy} \left(\mu \frac{dh}{dy}\right)  + \mu \left(\frac{du}{dy}\right)^2=0.</math>

where <math>\tau=\tau_w=\text{constant}</math> is the wall shear stress. The flow does not depend on the [[Reynolds number]] <math>\mathrm{Re}=U l/\nu_\infty</math>, but rather on the [[Prandtl number]] <math>\mathrm{Pr}=\mu_\infty c_{p\infty}/\kappa_\infty</math> and the [[Mach number]] <math>\mathrm{M} = U/c_\infty= U/\sqrt{(\gamma-1)h_\infty}</math>, where <math>\kappa</math> is the [[thermal conductivity]], <math>c</math> is the [[speed of sound]] and <math>\gamma</math> is the [[specific heat ratio]]. Introduce the non-dimensional variables

:<math>\tilde y = \frac{y}{l}, \quad \tilde T = \frac{T}{T_\infty}, \quad \tilde T_w = \frac{T_w}{T_\infty}, \quad \tilde h = \frac{h}{h_\infty}, \quad \tilde h_w= \frac{h_w}{h_\infty}, \quad \tilde u=\frac{u}{U}, \quad \tilde\mu = \frac{\mu}{\mu_\infty}, \quad \tilde\tau_w = \frac{\tau_w}{\mu_\infty U/l}</math>

In terms of these quantities, the solutions are

:<math>\tilde h = \tilde h_w + \left[\frac{\gamma-1}{2} \mathrm{M}^2 \mathrm{Pr} + (1-\tilde h_w)\right] \tilde u - \frac{\gamma-1}{2} \mathrm{M}^2 \mathrm{Pr} \, \tilde u^2,</math>
:<math>\tilde y = \frac{1}{\tilde \tau_w} \int_0^{\tilde u} \tilde \mu \, d\tilde u, \quad \tilde \tau_w =  \int_0^1 \tilde \mu \, d\tilde u, \quad q_w = - \frac{1}{\mathrm{Pr}} \tau_w \left(\frac{dh}{du}\right)_w,</math>

where <math>q_w</math> is the heat transferred per unit time per unit area from the lower wall. Thus <math>\tilde h, \tilde T, \tilde u, \tilde \mu</math> are implicit functions of <math>y</math>. One can also write the solution in terms of the recovery temperature <math>T_r</math> and recovery enthalpy <math>h_r</math> evaluated at the temperature of an insulated wall i.e., the values of <math>T_w</math> and <math>h_w</math> for which <math>q_w=0</math>.{{Clarify|date=December 2020}} Then the solution is

:<math>\frac{q_w}{\tau_w U} = \frac{\tilde T_w-\tilde T_r}{(\gamma-1)\mathrm{M}^2 \mathrm{Pr}}, \quad \tilde T_r =1+ \frac{\gamma-1}{2} \mathrm{M}^2\mathrm{Pr},</math>
:<math>\tilde h = \tilde h_w + (\tilde h_r-\tilde h_w) \tilde u - \frac{\gamma-1}{2}\mathrm{M}^2 \mathrm{Pr} \, \tilde u^2.</math>

If the [[specific heat]] is constant, then <math>\tilde h=\tilde T</math>. When <math>\mathrm{M}\rightarrow 0</math> and <math>T_w=T_\infty, \Rightarrow q_w= 0</math>, then <math>T</math> and <math>\mu</math> are constant everywhere, thus recovering the incompressible Couette flow solution. Otherwise, one must know the full temperature dependence of <math>\tilde \mu(\tilde T)</math>. While there is no simple expression for <math>\tilde \mu(\tilde T)</math> that is both accurate and general, there are several approximations for certain materials — see, e.g., [[temperature dependence of viscosity]]. When <math>\mathrm{M}\rightarrow 0</math> and <math>q_w\neq 0</math>, the recovery quantities become unity <math>\tilde T_r=1</math>. For air, the values <math>\gamma=1.4, \ \tilde \mu(\tilde T) = \tilde T^{2/3}</math> are commonly used, and the results for this case are shown in the figure.

The effects of [[Dissociation (chemistry)|dissociation]] and [[ionization]] (i.e., <math>c_p</math> is not constant) have also been studied; in that case the recovery temperature is reduced by the dissociation of molecules.<ref>Liepmann et al. (1956, 1957)</ref>

=== Rectangular channel ===
[[File:Couetter.pdf|thumb|200px|Couette flow for square channel]]
[[File:Couetter1.pdf|thumb|200px|Couette flow with h/l=0.1]]
One-dimensional flow <math>u(y)</math> is valid when both plates are infinitely long in the streamwise (<math>x</math>) and spanwise (<math>z</math>) directions. When the spanwise length is finite, the flow becomes two-dimensional and <math>u</math> is a function of both <math>y</math> and <math>z</math>. However, the infinite length in the streamwise direction must be retained in order to ensure the unidirectional nature of the flow.

As an example, consider an infinitely long rectangular channel with transverse height <math>h</math> and spanwise width <math>l</math>, subject to the condition that the top wall moves with a constant velocity <math>U</math>. Without an imposed pressure gradient, the Navier–Stokes equations reduce to

:<math>\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial z^2} =0</math>

with boundary conditions

:<math> u(0,z) =0, \quad u(h,z) = U,</math>
:<math> u(y,0) =0, \quad u(y,l) = 0.</math>

Using [[separation of variables]], the solution is given by

:<math>u(y,z) = \frac{4U}{\pi} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2n-1} \frac{\sinh (\beta_n y)}{\sinh (\beta_n h)} \sin (\beta_n z), \quad \beta_n = \frac{(2n-1)\pi}{l}.</math>

When <math>h/l\ll 1</math>, the planar Couette flow is recovered, as shown in the figure.

== Coaxial cylinders ==
[[Taylor–Couette flow]] is a flow between two rotating, infinitely long, coaxial cylinders.<ref>Landau and Lifshitz (1987)</ref> The original problem was solved by [[Sir George Stokes, 1st Baronet|Stokes]] in 1845,<ref>Stokes (1845)</ref> but [[Geoffrey Ingram Taylor]]'s name was attached to the flow because he studied its stability in a famous 1923 paper.<ref>Taylor (1923)</ref>

The problem can be solved in [[cylindrical coordinate]]s <math>(r, \theta, z)</math>. Denote the radii of the inner and outer cylinders as <math>R_1</math> and <math>R_2</math>. Assuming the cylinders rotate at constant angular velocities <math>\Omega_1</math> and <math>\Omega_2</math>, then the velocity in the <math>\theta</math>-direction is<ref>Guyon et al. (2001), pp. 163–166</ref>

:<math>v_\theta (r) = a r + \frac{b}{r} , \qquad a = \frac{\Omega_2 R_2^2-\Omega_1 R_1^2}{R_2^2-R_1^2}, \quad b = \frac{(\Omega_1-\Omega_2)R_1^2 R_2^2}{R_2^2-R_1^2}.</math>

This equation shows that the effects of curvature no longer allow for constant shear in the flow domain.

===Coaxial cylinders of finite length===
The classical Taylor–Couette flow problem assumes infinitely long cylinders; if the cylinders have non-negligible finite length <math>l</math>, then the analysis must be modified (though the flow is still unidirectional). For <math>\Omega_2=0</math>, the finite-length problem can be solved using [[separation of variables]] or [[integral transforms]], giving:<ref>Wendl (1999)</ref>

:<math>
v_\theta(r,z) = \frac{4R_1\Omega_1}{\pi} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2n-1} \frac{I_1(\beta_n  R_2) K_1(\beta_n  r) - K_1(\beta_n  R_2) I_1(\beta_n  r)}{I_1(\beta_n  R_2) K_1(\beta_n  R_1) - K_1(\beta_n  R_2) I_1(\beta_n  R_1)} \sin (\beta_n  z), \quad \beta_n = \frac{(2n-1)\pi}{l}, 
</math>

where <math>I(\beta_n r),\ K(\beta_nr)</math> are the [[Modified Bessel function]]s of the first and second kind.
